finding.title: OS Command Injection
finding.trigger: Passing attacker-controlled input directly to atoi without validation
finding.assumptions: The input is expected to be a valid integer, but no validation is performed to ensure it is within a reasonable range or format.

parsed.refutation_attempt: Checked that the sink function is atoi, which only parses a string into an integer and does not invoke any OS command execution primitives such as system(), exec(), or popen(). No subsequent code uses the parsed integer to construct or execute a shell command. Therefore the reported OS Command Injection claim is unfounded.

finding.title: Buffer Overflow
finding.trigger: Using untrusted input to allocate memory without checking if it is within a safe range
finding.assumptions: The input is expected to be a valid integer, but no validation is performed to ensure it is within a reasonable range or format.

parsed.refutation_attempt: Checked the code for any out‑of‑bounds array accesses. The loops that write to the matrices (lines 34‑40 and 42‑48) all use indices i,j,k that are bounded by N, which is the same value used to allocate the arrays (lines 23‑30). No indexing beyond the allocated size occurs, so there is no buffer overflow. The issue is an unchecked allocation size that could lead to integer overflow or memory exhaustion, but it does not cause a buffer overflow.

finding.title: OS Command Injection
finding.trigger: Passing attacker-controlled input directly to printMatrix without validation
finding.assumptions: The input is expected to be a valid integer, but no validation is performed to ensure it is within a reasonable range or format.

parsed.refutation_attempt: Checked the sink function printMatrix: it only uses printf with a format string "%d\t" to output integer values from the matrix. No system calls, exec, or command concatenation are performed. The source argv[1] is only converted to an integer N and used for array allocation and loop bounds, not passed to any command execution API. Therefore there is no path from untrusted input to an OS command execution. The claim of OS Command Injection is unfounded.

finding.title: OS Command Injection
finding.trigger: Passing attacker-controlled input directly to free without validation
finding.assumptions: The input is expected to be a valid integer, but no validation is performed to ensure it is within a reasonable range or format.

parsed.refutation_attempt: Checked the code for any path from the untrusted source argv[1] to the free calls. The source is parsed with atoi(argv[1]) to produce an integer N (line 20). This value is only used to determine the size of dynamically allocated matrices (lines 23‑30). The free calls (lines 56‑60) release memory that was allocated by malloc/calloc, not memory derived from argv[1]. No string or pointer derived from argv[1] is ever passed to free, and there is no command execution function involved. Therefore the claim of OS Command Injection via free is unfounded.
